source.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
source.authors: George Ma; Zhong-Yuan Liang; Irene Y. Chen; Somayeh Sojoudi

record.tranche_reason: The study refines claims about SAE features: its experiments find that contrastively selected reasoning-associated features often respond to lexical cues or fail under paraphrase, while its stylized analysis proposes a different sparsity-related mechanism. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a stylized mathematical analysis of sparse decoding, but it is not an experiment on overcomplete toy networks or superposition geometry. Steering results are described as an unreliable supplementary check on whether a feature encodes reasoning, so they are not recorded as evidence for the versions below. The study reports feature-selection and token-injection results by configuration; the LLM-guided falsification tables report analyzed/genuine/high-confidence counts.
record.test_reason: Only weakly. The empirical rows measure what drives contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning' features: token injection and LLM counterexamples. That is feature semantics, not the completeness, stability or canonicity V5 names. The part that bears on a version is the stylized theory (Sec. 3, Thm 3.1/B.3–B.4). It argues that l1 or Top-K sparse decoding keeps a stable 1-D cue while suppressing high-dimensional within-behavior variation, even with a perfect dictionary. That is a specific argument that SAE units can be incomplete for high-dimensional structure, so it is a T5 bearing on V5's 'complete' clause. No row captures it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that contrastive activation differences are not sufficient evidence for monosemantic reasoning features. Most candidates are token-sensitive, and the rest are falsified by targeted counterexamples and paraphrases. A stylized analysis suggests sparsity favors low-dimensional correlates. They scope the claim to individually selected features in their settings, explicitly do not rule out distributed or nonlinear reasoning representations, and recommend causal and adversarial validation.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes contrastively selected SAE features in LLMs, then applies token injection and LLM-guided counterexample generation. Its stylized orthonormal-dictionary sparse-decoding analysis is not the original Toy Models of Superposition method or a reproduction of its toy-network geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes varied by model, layer, reasoning dataset, and feature-ranking metric. Gemma-2 models had substantially weaker token-injection effects and more context-dependent candidates than many Gemma-3 configurations. The paper reports 45%–90% of candidates in token-driven categories across configurations; results using ROC-AUC and frequency-ratio ranking were described as qualitatively similar to Cohen’s d ranking.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 22 configurations, 45%–90% of top-100 contrastively selected 'reasoning' SAE features activate significantly when a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. Gemma-2 models are a weaker case, with 43–56% token-driven. All remaining context-dependent features analyzed (248 main-text, plus appendix models) admit LLM-generated false positives and meaning-preserving false-negative paraphrases. None qualify as genuine reasoning features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features selected by contrast for a high-level behavior (reasoning) mostly encode low-dimensional lexical or discourse correlates rather than the behavior itself.

fits_no_version.finding: Stylized theorem: l1 or Top-K sparse decoding with a perfect orthonormal dictionary suppresses high-dimensional isotropic within-behavior variation but retains a 1-D cue coordinate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparsity biases dictionary features toward low-dimensional correlates of behaviors whose variation is high-dimensional.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The theoretical account is explicitly stylized and does not characterize full SAE training dynamics. The empirical conclusions concern contrastively selected candidates and individual-feature interpretations, not distributed or nonlinear reasoning representations. LLM-guided falsification uses generated counterexamples; the authors report analyzing only sampled context-dependent features in some configurations. Gemma-2-9B Table 7 has an s1K count inconsistency: category counts sum to 78 although the experiment is described as selecting 100 features. Steering is small-scale and the authors caution that performance changes do not establish reasoning representation.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row cap. Steering benchmark results were not recorded because the authors state that steering performance is not a reliable indicator of whether a feature encodes reasoning, and the reported results do not directly test the listed versions.

untested.parts: No toy networks, superposition geometry, or sparsity-driven phase transition.
No test of capacity competition as a cause of polysemantic neurons.
Does not study neuron polysemanticity or its non-capacity causes.
Feature-detection values are selection statistics; the study does not test whether features are spread across neurons or whether SAEs recover the model's true sparse features.
Stability across SAE runs or sizes, canonicity, and empirical completeness (e.g., reconstruction or variance explained) are not measured. Only a stylized theoretical argument bears on completeness.
The theory contrasts a 1-D cue with a (k−1)-D isotropic component, but no empirical test of multi-dimensional versus 1-D features in models.

missing.what: Theoretical bounds on recovered energy of a (k−1)-D isotropic component under l1 (b²Ψ(u)) and Top-K (about K log k/k fraction) decoding, compared with cue recovery (Lemmas B.1–B.2).

record.verdict_notes: The link to the superposition versions is weak. The study is mainly about whether SAE features can be read as high-level behaviors. The reader's V4 'supports' rests on selection values and is removed. The reader's V5 'challenges' is replaced by a text-based limits_scope grounded in the theory, because the empirical rows do not measure completeness, stability or canonicity. Internal inconsistencies in the source: 248 versus 153 analyzed features (E.5); Table 7 s1K counts sum to 78; Fig. 9 mean 3.4 versus Table 14 mean 2.4. Steering results are correctly omitted.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test overcomplete toy networks, overlapping nearly orthogonal feature directions, sparsity-dependent geometric transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Does not study polysemantic neurons or establish that polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure.

Tests SAE feature activations that distinguish reasoning from non-reasoning text, but not whether reasoning information is distributed across neurons. Does not establish recovery of reasoning computations as opposed to linguistic correlates.

Tests selected contrastive SAE candidates for cue sensitivity and semantic invariance, not whether SAE features are complete, canonical, or stable across SAE training runs, dictionaries, or models generally.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features as the units of superposition.

rows.measure: Mean Cohen’s d of top 100 features

rows.subject: Gemma-3-12B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Inserted the feature’s top-associated tokens or n-grams into non-reasoning text; reports the strongest injection category per feature.
rows.measure: Number of top-100 features in token-driven, partially token-driven, weakly token-driven, and context-dependent categories; mean best-injection Cohen’s d
rows.baseline: Non-reasoning samples without inserted tokens
rows.value: 54, 10, 15, and 21 features, respectively; mean Cohen’s d 1.266
rows.uncertainty: Independent two-sample t-tests; category p-value thresholds stated as p < 0.01 or p < 0.05
rows.note: Token insertion induced significant activation for most selected candidates; a minority remained context-dependent.
rows.check: Token-injection categories show what triggers selected features (lexical cues versus context). They do not measure whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units. The 'partial' state against V5 has no meaning here. Record under fits_no_version. R37: Table 7 s1K counts (6+7+23+42) sum to 78, while the percentages sum to 100%; the inconsistency is in the source.

relationships.condition: Stylized orthonormal-dictionary model: a high-level behavior realized as high-dimensional isotropic variation, coupled with a stable 1-D cue, under l1 or Top-K sparse decoding.
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not rows (Sec. 3, Thm 3.1/B.4). Under sparse decoding, recovered energy from the (k−1)-D component decays exponentially, or is at most about K log k/k, while the cue is kept. So SAE features can be incomplete for high-dimensional structure. The empirical pattern in R21–R41 (cue-detector features, none tracking reasoning) is consistent with this. The authors say the theory is stylized and does not rule out distributed representation.
relationships.display_finding: Energy recovered from the (k−1)-dimensional component decayed exponentially or stayed at most about K log k/k while the cue was kept; observed features detected cues and none tracked reasoning, though the authors call the theory stylized.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Stylized orthonormal-dictionary model: a high-level behavior realized as high-dimensional isotropic variation, coupled with a stable 1-D cue, under l1 or Top-K sparse decoding.
source_check.reason: Theorem 3.1/B.3 bounds recovered residual energy by an exponentially decaying quantity; Theorem B.4 bounds its recovered fraction by order K log k/k. These establish conditional incompleteness; cue retention additionally requires the threshold or magnitude conditions in Lemmas B.1–B.2.

relation.reason: The study's own theoretical results bear on V5 completeness under the stated stylized conditions.

tranche.reason: Section 3 and Appendix B give a specific argument qualifying dictionary completeness: sparse decoding suppresses high-dimensional variation even with an ideal dictionary.

source_check.notes: The V5 evidence is stylized sparse-decoding theory, not an empirical completeness test. The reasoning-feature experiments do not isolate training-stage effects or test seed stability or canonicality.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: All feature-selection configurations reported in the main text and Appendix C
reader_labels.reason: Top-ranked SAE features showed reported mean Cohen’s d values of 0.602–1.043 for distinguishing reasoning from non-reasoning corpora, supporting the limited claim that SAE features can be recovered that discriminate these text sets (R01–R20).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Contrastively selected reasoning-associated candidates tested by token injection and LLM-guided falsification
reader_labels.reason: Token insertion activated many candidates without reasoning text, and the paper reports systematic false positives and meaning-preserving false negatives for all 248 context-dependent candidates, with none classified as genuine reasoning features (R21–R43).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: General claims about SAE features beyond the contrastively selected candidates and tested settings
reader_labels.reason: The evidence concerns selected reasoning-associated features and does not test completeness, canonical status, or stability across SAE dictionaries, training runs, or all model features (R21–R43).
